analysis.one_liner: Replaces employer-based health insurance with tax credits, guaranteed-issue private plans, Medicare copays, and malpractice limits.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Sen. Nickles with 24 Republican cosponsors, the bill got one Senate Finance Committee hearing in April 1994 and never a vote; the 103rd Congress ended with it still in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended the tax break for employer-provided health insurance and instead given individuals a refundable tax credit for premiums, requiring employers to pass the money through as wages. Insurers would have to sell a certified plan to anyone who applied, could not refuse renewal, and could only price by age, sex, and location. It paid for part of this by adding Medicare copayments, capping federal Medicaid payments, limiting malpractice awards, and exempting many hospital mergers and provider joint ventures from antitrust law.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and self-employed Americans would gain a refundable tax credit covering 25 to 75 percent of premiums and out-of-pocket costs, advanced through paychecks rather than waiting for tax season. People with preexisting conditions would gain guaranteed access to coverage at standard rates, with insurers barred from dropping them, and out-of-pocket costs capped. Low-income people would benefit from new state grants for coverage and preventive care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit for 25 to 75 percent of qualified health insurance premiums and unreimbursed medical costs, with the credit paid in advance through employers.

Requires federally qualified plans to issue coverage at standard rates to all applicants, guarantee renewability, and limit premium rating to age, sex, and geography, with an annual out-of-pocket cap of at least $5,000 per family.
Requires employers to withhold and remit premiums to the worker's chosen plan, add the employer's health contribution to cash wages, and hold workers harmless for the resulting payroll taxes.
Provides grants to states for health insurance coverage, acute medical services, and preventive care for low-income individuals.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries would face new 20 percent copayments for laboratory services, many home health visits, and skilled nursing care. Hospitals would lose disproportionate-share payments that compensate for treating low-income patients, and federal Medicaid payments for acute care would be capped. People injured by medical negligence would have damages and attorney fees limited, and consumers would have less recourse against provider consolidation because hospital mergers and joint ventures would gain antitrust safe harbors. State laws mandating benefits or restricting managed care would be preempted.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare seniors, safety-net hospitals, malpractice victims

drawbacks.text: Imposes new Medicare copayments of 20 percent on laboratory services, certain home health visits, and skilled nursing facility care, shifting costs onto seniors.

Caps federal Medicaid payments for acute care services and ends disproportionate-share hospital payments under both Medicare and Medicaid, cutting funds that safety-net hospitals rely on to serve low-income patients.

Limits damages, non-economic awards, and attorney fees in malpractice cases, immunizes FDA-approved products from punitive damages, and shields hospital mergers and provider joint ventures from antitrust review, reducing accountability for patients.
Preempts state laws mandating specific insurance benefits and restricting managed care practices, overriding consumer protections states had enacted.
Terminates the tax exclusion for employer-provided insurance and the medical expense deduction after 1997, so workers would pay tax on the cashed-out value of their health benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real: guaranteed issue, guaranteed renewability, community-style rating, and out-of-pocket caps would have addressed the worst problems of the 1994 individual insurance market, and the refundable credit would have reached people employers did not cover. But the bill's financing leaned on cost-shifting: seniors would pay more out of pocket, hospitals serving the poor would lose federal payments, and the bill traded away malpractice accountability and antitrust enforcement to win provider acceptance. Whether the tax credits would have made coverage affordable for low-income families was untested, and the bill itself required a report, five years after enactment, on how many Americans ended up forgoing insurance entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, got a single hearing in April 1994, and sat there until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 without ever reaching the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Don Nickles introduced the bill on November 20, 1993, with 24 Republican cosponsors including Sens. Dole, Hatch, Lott, and Grassley, as the Republicans' market-based alternative during the 1994 health reform debate.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on November 20, 1993.
The Finance Committee held hearings on the bill on April 26, 1994, and a star print (a corrected reprint) was ordered on June 16, 1994, but the committee never reported the bill.
No further action was taken; the bill remained in committee when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and died without a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No health system overhaul of any kind passed in 1994, so private insurers, employers, and the existing insurance market continued unchanged, while millions of uninsured Americans gained nothing. The bill's backers also lost, since their alternative never reached the floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent insurers and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Don Nickles
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 24 of 43 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including party leaders Sen. Dole and Sen. Lott.

against.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on the bill but never scheduled a committee markup or vote, leaving it unreported at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. George Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Championed the Clinton administration's competing universal-coverage plan and never brought this alternative to the Senate floor.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Pushed his own Health Security Act as the vehicle for health reform, against which this bill was the Republican counterproposal.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 original cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic majority that controlled the Finance Committee chairmanship and the Senate calendar never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill keeps private insurance as the only channel for coverage: employers must remit premiums to the insurer each worker chooses, and employer group plans convert to certified private plans. In exchange, insurers must accept all applicants at standard rates and cannot cancel coverage, trading guaranteed-issue obligations for a permanently enlarged, federally protected individual market.

The bill carves antitrust safe harbors for hospital mergers, high-technology joint ventures, joint purchasing, and provider negotiations, and caps malpractice damages while barring punitive damages against FDA-approved products. Providers gain consolidation freedom and litigation protection that ordinary patients bear through higher prices and limited compensation.

The bill eliminates Medicare and Medicaid disproportionate-share payments, which compensate hospitals for treating low-income and uninsured patients, and caps federal Medicaid acute-care payments. The bill's own structure pushes the previously uninsured into private plans, but the cuts land on hospitals serving the poor in the transition.

Employers would stop providing health coverage as a benefit and instead add the value of their contribution to workers' wages while withholding premiums for each worker's chosen plan. They shed a costly benefit obligation but take on new payroll and reporting duties backed by $50-per-day excise taxes for noncompliance.
